title: The chemistry of wine
description: From must to glass: how sugars, acids, alcohol and oxygen shape style and quality

lessons.title: Sugar and alcohol
lessons.intro: Every alcohol level comes from vineyard and cellar choices: understanding sugar-to-alcohol conversion helps you read a wine style.
lessons.final: Now you can connect grape ripeness and alcoholic strength in the glass.

questions.question: During fermentation, yeasts mainly convert:
All else being equal, more sugar in must can lead to more alcohol.
A wine from very ripe grapes tends to have:

slides.title: From sugar to ABV
paragraphs: In must, sugar concentration tells you how much raw material yeasts can use to produce alcohol.
That is why later harvests can create richer, higher-alcohol wines, while earlier harvests often produce leaner and sharper profiles.

slides.title: Practical case: two Pinot Grigio wines
paragraphs: Pinot Grigio A: earlier harvest, 12% ABV, citrus-driven and light.
Pinot Grigio B: riper harvest, 13.5% ABV, softer texture and warmer finish.

lessons.title: Acidity and freshness
lessons.intro: Acidity is not a flaw: it is the engine of drinkability, especially in whites and sparkling wines.
lessons.final: Now you can separate true freshness from simple lightness.

questions.question: In tasting, good acidity mainly increases:
A wine with no acidity can feel flat and tired.
Which style often needs marked acidity for balance?

slides.title: Why acidity matters
paragraphs: Tartaric, malic and citric acids are natural grape components that support wine over time.
On the palate, acidity drives another sip and improves compatibility with food.

slides.title: Quick pairing test
paragraphs: A crisp white (for example young Verdicchio) refreshes the palate with fried seafood.
A low-acid white with the same dish can feel heavy after a few bites.

lessons.title: pH and stability
lessons.intro: pH is a small number with major impact: microbial stability, color behavior and aging potential all depend on it.
lessons.final: Now you can read pH as a practical cellar indicator, not just a theory term.

questions.question: A lower pH generally indicates:
pH can influence color stability in red wines.
In the cellar, overly high pH raises the risk of:

slides.title: pH vs total acidity
paragraphs: Total acidity and pH describe different aspects: quantity of acids versus their chemical strength and sensory impact.
Two wines with similar acidity can taste very different if pH is not aligned.

slides.title: Operational example
paragraphs: Young red at pH 3.35: brighter color and tighter profile.
Similar red at pH 3.75: less vivid color and higher long-term vulnerability.

lessons.title: Tannins: structure and texture
lessons.intro: Saying 'tannic' is not enough: tannin quality ranges from green and harsh to ripe and silky.
lessons.final: Now you can evaluate tannins by texture, not just intensity.

questions.question: The classic tannin sensation is:
Good phenolic ripeness can make tannins feel smoother.
In red wines, tannins mostly come from:

slides.title: Where tannins come from
paragraphs: Extracted during maceration and fermentation, tannins build structure and aging potential.
Careful temperature and pump-over management helps avoid bitter, aggressive extraction.

slides.title: Service vocabulary
paragraphs: 'Polished tannins' means a fine, less abrasive grain on gums and tongue.
'Green tannins' describes a dry, hard texture, often linked to incomplete grape ripeness.

lessons.title: Alcohol and heat perception
lessons.intro: Alcohol affects body, perceived sweetness and warmth: balance with acidity and tannin is essential.
lessons.final: Now you know when alcohol supports a wine and when it dominates it.

questions.question: On the palate, alcohol typically creates:
Higher ABV often needs stronger freshness to remain balanced.
Which pairing helps with a high-alcohol red?

slides.title: Alcohol is more than a number
paragraphs: As ABV rises, volume and roundness can increase, but so can the risk of a hot and unbalanced finish.
Serving temperature can moderate alcohol perception and protect aromatic precision.

slides.title: Tasting comparison
paragraphs: Wine A at 12.5%: leaner, more vertical, drier finish.
Wine B at 15%: fuller and broader, best balanced by rich food or vivid acidity.

lessons.title: Carbon dioxide (CO2)
lessons.intro: CO2 is not only for sparkling wine: even still wines can show it and change mouthfeel.
lessons.final: Now you can tell when CO2 is a stylistic plus and when it becomes a flaw.

questions.question: Residual CO2 in a still wine can give:
Only sparkling wines can contain carbon dioxide.
CO2 mainly originates from:

slides.title: Origin and function of CO2
paragraphs: Alcoholic fermentation naturally produces CO2, and a small portion may remain dissolved in wine.
In some young whites, a slight amount increases freshness and palate tension.

slides.title: When it is too much
paragraphs: If CO2 is excessive in a wine meant to be still, it can mask delicate aromas and feel unfinished.
Proper maturation and bottling management helps prevent this issue.

lessons.title: Oxygen and oxidation
lessons.intro: Oxygen helps in small doses, but excess exposure can quickly push wine toward decline.
lessons.final: Now you can separate useful micro-oxygenation from harmful oxidation.

questions.question: Too much oxygen is most likely to cause:
A little oxygen can help soften some red wines.
A classic sign of advanced oxidation is:

slides.title: Dose and timing of oxygen
paragraphs: During racking, aging or service, oxygen always changes wine profile; it is never neutral.
Structured reds may benefit from moderate oxygen contact, while delicate whites have a much narrower margin.

slides.title: Restaurant service example
paragraphs: Decanting a young, closed red can improve aromatic opening.
Leaving an aromatic white exposed for hours can flatten and dull its profile.

lessons.title: Residual sugar and style
lessons.intro: Residual sugar is not only about sweetness: it also affects body, balance and aromatic expression.
lessons.final: Now you can clearly explain dry, off-dry and sweet styles.

questions.question: Residual sugar is:
answers: Sugar found only in red wine

questions.question: A wine can feel less sweet if acidity is high, even with small residual sugar.
In which style is residual sugar often intentionally preserved?

slides.title: Dry does not mean absolute zero sugar
paragraphs: Many dry wines still contain small residual sugar amounts without tasting sweet.
Final perception depends on balance with acidity, alcohol and serving temperature.

slides.title: Guest-friendly explanation
paragraphs: If a guest asks for 'not too sweet', suggest a wine with low residual sugar and vivid acidity.
If they ask for a softer profile, a slight residue can round the palate without becoming dessert-like.

lessons.title: Sulfur dioxide (SO2)
lessons.intro: SO2 is a protective tool: the real question is dose, timing and purpose, not slogans.
lessons.final: Now you can discuss SO2 with technical clarity and no alarmism.

questions.question: The main role of SO2 in wine is:
'No sulfites added' does not automatically mean better wine in every case.
Correct SO2 management aims for:

slides.title: Free SO2 and total SO2
paragraphs: Free SO2 is the active fraction that actually protects wine and aromas.
Good pH control and cellar hygiene often allow lower doses while keeping safety and stability.

slides.title: Balanced message
paragraphs: With guests, avoid extremes: explain SO2 as a seatbelt for wine integrity.
Low or high alone is not the whole story; what matters is in-glass quality over time.

lessons.title: Final chemical balance
lessons.intro: A compelling wine does not win on one parameter alone: it succeeds when all components work together.
lessons.final: Now you can evaluate chemical-sensory harmony as a true quality criterion.

questions.question: A balanced wine shows:
Too much of one component can reduce drinkability and harmony.
Which professional summary best describes balance?

slides.title: The harmony formula
paragraphs: Acidity, alcohol, tannins, residual sugar and aroma profile should support each other.
When one voice overwhelms the others, the wine loses precision and easy drinkability.

slides.title: Taster checklist
paragraphs: Ask yourself: is the sip coherent from attack to finish? is it clean? do aromas return clearly?
If yes, you are likely tasting a wine with strong technical and sensory balance.
